paragraphs.heading: Rivers of fast air
paragraphs.text: Jet streams are narrow, fast-moving currents of air. On Earth the main ones sit near the height of the tropopause and blow from west to east around the globe. Each hemisphere has a polar jet circling its polar vortex about 9.1 km (30,000 ft) above sea level, usually moving at around 180 km/h (110 mph) and often much faster. Nearer the equator, a little higher and a little weaker, runs the subtropical jet.

paragraphs.heading: Where they come from
paragraphs.text: Two things produce the polar and subtropical jets. Sunlight heats the atmosphere and sets up the big polar, Ferrel and Hadley circulation cells, and the Coriolis force, which comes from the planet spinning on its axis, acts on that moving air. The polar jet forms near the border between the polar and Ferrel cells, mostly between latitudes 30° and 60° and closer to 60°. The subtropical jet forms near the border between the Ferrel and Hadley cells, close to 30°. In some places and times the two jets merge, while at others they stay well apart.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and movement
paragraphs.text: A jet is usually a few hundred kilometres wide and often less than five kilometres thick. It tends to wind along a meandering path, and the bends drift eastward more slowly than the wind inside them. Each large bend is called a Rossby wave, or planetary wave, and these waves arise because the Coriolis effect changes with latitude. Winds are fastest where neighbouring air masses differ most in temperature, and speeds of 400 km/h (250 mph) have been measured. In the north, the polar jet is said to "follow the sun", creeping north as the hemisphere warms and back south as it cools.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: As they move from west to east, jet streams bring changes in the weather. Forecasters use the position of some jets to help predict it, and the lower polar jets, which often push into the mid-latitudes, strongly affect both weather and flying. Airlines ride them to shorten some flights and burn less fuel. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation shifts where the jets lie, which changes the weather over the tropical Pacific and the climate across much of the tropics and subtropics.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the jet stream
paragraphs.text: The American professor Elias Loomis (1811–1889) gave the first hints, suggesting a strong west-to-east current high over the United States to explain how major storms behaved. In the 1920s the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi tracked pilot balloons rising near Mount Fuji and detected the jet stream. He published in Esperanto, so his work went largely unnoticed outside Japan, yet by date he should be credited with the scientific discovery. In 1939 the German meteorologist Heinrich Seilkopf coined the word Strahlströmung, meaning "jet current".

paragraphs.heading: Wartime and other worlds
paragraphs.text: Many credit real understanding of jet streams to repeated flights during World War II, when crews kept meeting westerly tailwinds above 160 km/h (100 mph), for instance flying from the US to the UK. In 1944 American meteorologists on Guam, Reid Bryson among them, could forecast strong west winds that would slow bombers raiding Japan. Japan used the jet stream too, sending Fu-Go balloon bombs across the Pacific to make small attacks on North America. Jet streams have also been detected on Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
